snapshots.name: John Field
snapshots.body: An honest, hard-working, but shiftless Irish tenant farmer at the Baker Farm, visited during a thunderstorm in Chapter 10; Thoreau tries, without success, to persuade him that his laborious pursuit of tea, coffee, and meat is what keeps him poor.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Cato
snapshots.body: Marcus Porcius Cato the Elder, the Roman statesman and agricultural writer, quoted four times on farming and household management from his De Re Rustica -- including the recipe Thoreau follows for his own kneaded bread. Never confused in the text with Cato Ingraham, the formerly enslaved Concord resident of Chapter 14, who is bound separately and carries no global alias.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Cato Ingraham
snapshots.body: A formerly enslaved man, held by Duncan Ingraham of Concord village, who built him a house and let him live in Walden Woods; Thoreau notes the half-obliterated cellar hole that was his home, and that he is not to be confused with either Roman Cato -- "Cato, not Uticensis, but Concordiensis."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Brister Freeman
snapshots.body: A formerly enslaved man, "a handy Negro," held by Squire Cummings, who planted the apple trees still bearing wild fruit on Brister's Hill; his gravestone in the old Lincoln burying-ground styles him "Sippio Brister" -- a name Thoreau hears echoing Scipio Africanus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Fenda
snapshots.body: Brister Freeman's wife, "large, round, and black," who told fortunes hospitably and shared his house on Brister's Hill.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Zilpha
snapshots.body: A colored woman who spun linen for the townsfolk in a small house near Thoreau's bean-field, singing shrilly as she worked; her dwelling was burned by English prisoners of war in 1812 while she was away, killing her cat, dog, and hens.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hugh Quoil
snapshots.body: The last inhabitant of Walden Woods before Thoreau, an Irish ditcher known as "Col. Quoil," reputed to have fought at Waterloo; a man of manners and civil speech despite his poverty and trembling delirium, he died in the road at the foot of Brister's Hill shortly after Thoreau's arrival.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: John Farmer
snapshots.body: A parable figure of Chapter 11: a laborer who, resting after a hard day's work, hears a flute and feels called to a higher life than his "mean moiling" one, though he cannot see how to answer the call beyond a new austerity of mind.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hermit
snapshots.body: Thoreau's own voice in Chapter 12's staged dialogue -- a would-be contemplative interrupted mid-meditation by the Poet's proposal to go fishing, and unable to resist.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Poet
snapshots.body: The Hermit's fishing companion in Chapter 12's staged dialogue, identified with no other name; real-world scholarship reads him as Thoreau's friend and fellow writer William Ellery Channing, but the text itself never supplies that name.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Duncan Ingraham
snapshots.body: A gentleman of Concord village who enslaved Cato Ingraham and built him the house in Walden Woods where he was permitted to live.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Squire Cummings
snapshots.body: The Concord man who enslaved Brister Freeman.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: the Stratton family
snapshots.body: A former-inhabitant family whose homestead and orchard once covered the slope of Brister's Hill, named only by surname, with no individual member identified; not to be confused with Hezekiah Stratton, named later in the ledger excerpt of Chapter 15.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: the Breed family
snapshots.body: A former-inhabitant family whose hut, the site of a famous local house-fire Thoreau describes at length, stood near the edge of the wood closer to the village.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Nutting and Le Grosse
snapshots.body: Two former inhabitants named together, who lived where a well and lilac bushes still mark an open field; nothing else is told of them. Not to be confused with Sam Nutting, named later in Chapter 15.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Wyman the potter
snapshots.body: A potter who squatted farther into the woods than any other former inhabitant, furnished the town with earthenware, and left descendants who continued the trade after him; the last inhabitant before Hugh Quoil, who occupied "Wyman's tenement."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Wyman the younger
snapshots.body: Wyman the potter's descendant, who continued the family trade and later disappeared; a travelling pottery-dealer who had once bought a wheel from him stops to ask Thoreau what became of him.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Sam Nutting
snapshots.body: A bear-hunter on Fair Haven Ledges who traded skins for rum in Concord village and once claimed to have seen a moose there; owner of the famous fox-hound Burgoyne. Not to be confused with the unrelated former-inhabitant family of the same surname in Chapter 14.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Burgoyne
snapshots.body: Sam Nutting's famous fox-hound, borrowed by Thoreau's informant; Nutting himself pronounced the name "Bugine."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hezekiah Stratton
snapshots.body: A Concord man credited in an old trader's ledger with a wild-cat skin in 1743; a sergeant in the French war, and so not one who would have gotten credit for hunting less noble game. Not to be confused with the unrelated Stratton family of Chapter 14.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: John Melven
snapshots.body: A Concord man credited in an old trader's ledger with a grey fox skin in January 1742/3.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Mr. Gilian Baker
snapshots.body: A Lincoln farmer near the pond whose household kept an unusual "winged cat," which Thoreau visited and describes in Chapter 12.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Mr. Coleman
snapshots.body: Henry Coleman, the Massachusetts agricultural commissioner whose published farm reports Thoreau twice notes did not cover his bean-field.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Luther Blanchard
snapshots.body: A Concord Minuteman wounded at the Battle of Concord, invoked as a point of comparison in the mock-heroic account of Thoreau's ant battle.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Buttrick
snapshots.body: Major John Buttrick, who commanded the Concord Minutemen at the North Bridge; his order "Fire! for God's sake fire!" is echoed in the mock-heroic account of Thoreau's ant battle.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Davis and Hosmer
snapshots.body: Isaac Davis and Abner Hosmer, the two Concord Minutemen killed at the Battle of Concord, named together as the human dead whose fate the ant battle's carnage is mock-heroically compared to.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Homer
snapshots.body: The Greek epic poet; Thoreau keeps the Iliad on his table through the summer, reads a passage of it aloud in translation to a woodchopper acquaintance, and cites Alexander's habit of carrying it on campaign.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Æschylus
snapshots.body: The Greek tragedian, named alongside Homer as a classic never yet printed in English translation worth the name.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Virgil
snapshots.body: The Roman poet, named alongside Homer and Æschylus as a classic author.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Alexander
snapshots.body: Alexander the Great, who is said to have carried the Iliad with him on his expeditions in a precious casket.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Mîr Camar Uddîn Mast
snapshots.body: A poet Thoreau quotes on the pleasure of reading, comparing it to intoxication by wine.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Damodara
snapshots.body: An epithet of Krishna in Hindu scripture; Thoreau quotes a saying attributed to him about the freedom of a vast horizon, spoken when his herds needed new pastures.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: king Tching-thang
snapshots.body: A legendary Chinese emperor (Tang of Shang); Thoreau cites the characters said to be engraved on his bathing tub, urging daily renewal.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Confucius
snapshots.body: The Chinese philosopher, quoted several times under different transliterations of his name (Confucius, Khoung-tseu, Con-fut-see) on knowledge, virtue, and neighborliness.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Kieou-he-yu
snapshots.body: A great dignitary of the state of Wei, in the anecdote Thoreau quotes about sending a messenger to Confucius for news of his master.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Plato
snapshots.body: The Athenian philosopher; Thoreau reproaches himself for having his Dialogues on the shelf and never reading them, and later discusses Plato's definition of man as "a biped without feathers."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Zoroaster
snapshots.body: The ancient Persian religious teacher, invoked as an example of someone who had the same spiritual experience as a solitary hired man Thoreau knows, but treated it as universal wisdom rather than private singularity.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Jesus Christ
snapshots.body: Named as one through whose liberalizing influence, along with all the worthies, a solitary man might commune and set aside sectarian religion.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Abelard
snapshots.body: Peter Abelard, the medieval philosopher; Thoreau asks whether Concord could not hire some Abelard to lecture to it, as part of his argument that villages should fund culture as noblemen once did.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Adam
snapshots.body: The first man of Genesis, cited as the origin of human tedium and ennui, and, with Eve, of the first clothing (the bower) worn before the Fall.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Eve
snapshots.body: The first woman of Genesis, named with Adam as driven from Eden, and as first wearing the bower of Paradise before any other clothing.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Adam Smith
snapshots.body: The Scottish economist, named alongside Ricardo and Say as the "political economy" a poor student is taught in college while graduating in debt.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Ricardo
snapshots.body: David Ricardo, the British economist, named alongside Adam Smith and Say.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Say
snapshots.body: Jean-Baptiste Say, the French economist, named alongside Adam Smith and Ricardo. His surname also happens to be an ordinary English verb, capitalized twice elsewhere at the start of a sentence; only this one mention names the economist.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Sir Kenelm Digby
snapshots.body: The seventeenth-century English natural philosopher, quoted on the "vital spirits" attracted by fallow, exhausted soil.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Kirby
snapshots.body: William Kirby, co-author with Spence of a standard entomology text, cited on insects' feeding habits and on the history of recorded ant battles.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Spence
snapshots.body: William Spence, Kirby's co-author, cited alongside him.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Thseng-tseu
snapshots.body: Zengzi, a disciple of Confucius, quoted on the soul's absence from itself when the appetite masters perception: "one eats, and one does not know the savor of food."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Mencius
snapshots.body: The Chinese philosopher, quoted on the thin margin that distinguishes men from brute beasts, and how easily the common herd loses it.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Chaucer’s nun
snapshots.body: The Canterbury Tales narrator Thoreau quotes and attributes to "Chaucer's nun," on hunters not being unholy men. Chaucer's own name never appears in the text on its own -- only as part of this one phrase -- so there is no separate entry for Chaucer himself.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Huber
snapshots.body: François Huber, the Swiss entomologist Kirby and Spence credit as the only modern author to have witnessed a battle of ants firsthand.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Æneas Sylvius
snapshots.body: Aeneas Sylvius Piccolomini, later Pope Pius II, quoted by Kirby and Spence for his circumstantial account of a battle of ants on a pear tree.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Eugenius the Fourth
snapshots.body: Pope Eugene IV, in whose pontificate the ant battle Æneas Sylvius describes is said to have taken place.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Nicholas Pistoriensis
snapshots.body: An eminent lawyer said to have witnessed and related the history of the ant battle Æneas Sylvius describes.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Olaus Magnus
snapshots.body: The Swedish churchman and writer who records a second ant battle, quoted by Kirby and Spence.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Christiern the Second
snapshots.body: Christian II of Denmark, the "tyrant" whose expulsion from Sweden the ant battle Olaus Magnus describes is said to have preceded.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Polk
snapshots.body: James K. Polk, President of the United States when Thoreau's own witnessed ant battle took place, per his mock-scholarly dating of the event.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Webster
snapshots.body: Daniel Webster, whose Fugitive-Slave Bill dates Thoreau's ant battle in Chapter 12, and who is later named, in Chapter 18, as the orator of an imagined national celebration presided over by God.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Samuel Laing
snapshots.body: The travel writer quoted on Laplanders sleeping unclothed on snow in reindeer-skin bags.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Winslow
snapshots.body: Edward Winslow, later governor of the Plymouth Colony, whose account of a diplomatic visit to Massasoit -- warmly received but poorly fed and lodged -- Thoreau quotes at length.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Massasoit
snapshots.body: The Wampanoag sachem who received Winslow's Plymouth delegation, sharing what little food his people had.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Benvenuto Cellini
snapshots.body: The Italian Renaissance artist and memoirist, whose account of a halo seen over his own shadow after a vision in prison Thoreau compares to a phenomenon he has observed himself.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Guy Faux
snapshots.body: Guy Fawkes, the Gunpowder Plot conspirator, named in a quoted poem about the Baker Farm.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: William Gilpin
snapshots.body: The English writer on landscape aesthetics, quoted on the dimensions and origin of Scotland's Loch Fyne, used as a point of comparison for Walden's own depth.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Michaux
snapshots.body: François André Michaux, the French botanist, quoted on the high price of firewood in early-nineteenth-century New York and Philadelphia.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Nebuchadnezzar
snapshots.body: The Babylonian king; Thoreau notes, of his second-hand chimney bricks, that he did not find this name inscribed on them, unlike the ancient bricks of Babylon that supply Mesopotamian villages with building material.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Franklin
snapshots.body: Sir John Franklin, the British Arctic explorer whose lost expedition was a major contemporary news story; Thoreau asks pointedly whether he is "the only man who is lost."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Mr. Grinnell
snapshots.body: Henry Grinnell, the American philanthropist who funded search expeditions for Sir John Franklin.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Mungo Park
snapshots.body: The Scottish explorer of West Africa, named among the explorers Thoreau urges his reader to become instead within their own mind.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Lewis
snapshots.body: Meriwether Lewis, of the Lewis and Clark expedition, named among the explorers of Chapter 18's closing exhortation.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Clarke
snapshots.body: William Clark, of the Lewis and Clark expedition, named alongside Lewis.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Frobisher
snapshots.body: Sir Martin Frobisher, the English explorer who searched for the Northwest Passage, named among Chapter 18's explorers.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Columbus
snapshots.body: Christopher Columbus, invoked as the model for exploring continents and worlds within oneself rather than geographic ones.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Mirabeau
snapshots.body: The Comte de Mirabeau, quoted on having taken to highway robbery to test what resolution was needed to defy society's most sacred laws -- a resolve Thoreau calls manly but idle.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Kabir
snapshots.body: The Indian poet-saint, whose verses are said to admit four different senses -- cited as a contrast to the demand, in Thoreau's own place and time, that writing admit only one interpretation.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Crœsus
snapshots.body: The proverbially wealthy king of Lydia, invoked to argue that even his riches would not change what a person's true aims and means must be.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Tom Hyde
snapshots.body: A tinker, hanged, whose last words on the gallows -- reminding tailors to knot their thread before the first stitch -- Thoreau offers as an example of truth over decorum.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Champollion
snapshots.body: Jean-François Champollion, decipherer of Egyptian hieroglyphics, invoked rhetorically to ask who will decipher the "hieroglyphic" of the sand foliage on the railroad bank.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Calidas
snapshots.body: Kalidasa, the classical Sanskrit poet and dramatist, whose play Sacontala Thoreau quotes for its image of golden pollen-dust.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Jupiter
snapshots.body: The chief god of the Roman pantheon; commerce, Thoreau notes, does not clasp its hands and pray to him, and Hebe, cupbearer to Jupiter, is invoked as a symbol of perpetual youth and health.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Ceres
snapshots.body: The Roman goddess of agriculture, to whom -- Thoreau argues -- modern farmers no longer sacrifice, worshipping the infernal Plutus instead.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Plutus
snapshots.body: The Greek god of wealth, whom Thoreau says the modern farmer serves in place of Ceres.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Saturn
snapshots.body: The Roman god of a legendary golden age, named as the ancestral king whose race the old Romans believed themselves alone left of, and again as the "prostrate Saturn of an older dynasty" one steps over on entering Thoreau's imagined communal hall.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Minerva
snapshots.body: The Roman goddess of wisdom, invoked in an anecdote about her objection to a house Momus criticized for not being movable, and again as the master builder of an oil-and-wine-cellar-equipped villa.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Aurora
snapshots.body: The Roman goddess of the dawn; Thoreau calls himself as sincere a worshipper of her as the Greeks, and all poets and heroes are called her children.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Memnon
snapshots.body: The mythological son of Aurora, a byword for a statue that sang at dawn; invoked as the type of all poets and heroes, children of Aurora who emit their music at sunrise.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hygeia
snapshots.body: The Greek goddess of health, daughter of Æsculapius; Thoreau declines to worship her, preferring Hebe instead.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Æsculapius
snapshots.body: The Greek and Roman god of medicine, named as Hygeia's father, "that old herb-doctor."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hebe
snapshots.body: The Roman goddess of youth, cupbearer to Jupiter and daughter of Juno; Thoreau prefers her worship to Hygeia's, calling her the power to restore gods and men to the vigor of youth.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Juno
snapshots.body: The Roman queen of the gods, named as Hebe's mother.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Atlas
snapshots.body: The Titan condemned to bear the world on his shoulders, invoked when Thoreau describes his own eagerness to improve the Hollowell farm.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hercules
snapshots.body: The Greek and Roman demigod hero; his twelve labors are compared, unfavorably, to the burdens Thoreau's Concord neighbors have undertaken, and his strength is invoked again when Thoreau feels "strength like Antæus" from his beans.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Cerberus
snapshots.body: The three-headed dog guarding the underworld in Greek myth, invoked as a figure for any host's overbearing insistence on feeding a guest.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Vulcan
snapshots.body: The Roman god of fire, to whom Thoreau says he sacrificed an old forest fence for firewood.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Terminus
snapshots.body: The Roman god of boundaries, whom an old forest fence, past its usefulness, was said no longer to serve.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Brahma
snapshots.body: The Hindu creator god, invoked in the parable of the artist of Kouroo, whose perfect staff becomes, at the moment of completion, one of the fairest of all of Brahma's creations.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Vishnu
snapshots.body: The Hindu preserver god, named alongside Brahma and Indra as a deity the servant of a Brahmin priest is said to worship.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Indra
snapshots.body: The Hindu king of the gods, named alongside Brahma and Vishnu, and invoked earlier as the detached spectator in the sky Thoreau imagines himself as, watching the stream of events from above.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Thor
snapshots.body: The Norse god of thunder, whose hammer -- which only breaks things in pieces -- is contrasted with the gentler, more powerful persuasion of the spring thaw.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Atropos
snapshots.body: One of the three Fates in Greek myth, who cuts the thread of life; Thoreau proposes her name for the unstoppable railroad engine, "a fate ... that never turns aside."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Ulysses
snapshots.body: The hero of Homer's Odyssey, invoked as the model for sailing past the daily "whirlpool" of dinner "tied to the mast," resisting distraction.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Achilles
snapshots.body: The hero of Homer's Iliad; Thoreau translates his rebuke to Patroclus aloud to a woodchopper acquaintance, and later imagines a red ant as "some Achilles" avenging a fallen companion in the battle of the ants.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Patroclus
snapshots.body: Achilles' companion in the Iliad, whose sad countenance Achilles rebukes in the passage Thoreau translates aloud, and whom the avenging red ant of the battle scene is compared to avenging.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Menœtius
snapshots.body: Patroclus's father, named in the Iliad passage Thoreau translates.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Peleus
snapshots.body: Achilles' father, named in the same Iliad passage.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Æacus
snapshots.body: Peleus's father and Achilles' grandfather, named in the same Iliad passage.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: the Myrmidons
snapshots.body: Achilles' warriors in the Iliad, named in the translated passage; Thoreau later calls the legions of battling ants in his wood-yard "these Myrmidons."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Antæus
snapshots.body: The giant of Greek myth who drew his strength from contact with the earth; Thoreau says he got strength like his from cultivating his bean rows.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: the Sirens
snapshots.body: The mythological singers whose voices lured sailors to their deaths; Thoreau says he escapes the village's gossip by keeping his thoughts on high things, "like Orpheus," who drowned their voices with his own song.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Orpheus
snapshots.body: The legendary musician of Greek myth, whose singing drowned out the Sirens' voices and kept him out of danger, a model Thoreau invokes for escaping the village's gossip.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Robinhood
snapshots.body: The legendary English outlaw, named among those across history and rank who have all required a few sticks from the forest to warm them and cook their food.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Goody Blake
snapshots.body: A character from Wordsworth's poem "Goody Blake and Harry Gill," named alongside Harry Gill in the same passage as Robinhood.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Harry Gill
snapshots.body: The other title character of Wordsworth's poem, named alongside Goody Blake.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Actæon
snapshots.body: The mythological hunter torn apart by his own hounds; Thoreau notes that the woods ring with hunting cries yet no fox bursts forth "pursuing their Actæon."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Toscar
snapshots.body: A figure from the Ossianic poems, named as the father of the "beautiful daughter" mourned in a quoted verse.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Pilpay
snapshots.body: The legendary Indian fabulist credited with the beast-fables of the Panchatantra, invoked (as "Pilpay & Co.") for having put animals to their best literary use as vehicles for human thought.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Robin Goodfellow
snapshots.body: The mischievous sprite of English folklore (later Shakespeare's Puck), invoked as a figure for an erratic, meddling sun that helps by fits and starts rather than steadily.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Reynard
snapshots.body: The fox of medieval beast-fable tradition, invoked generically for the fox a black chicken at Hugh Quoil's abandoned house is said to be "awaiting."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Tell
snapshots.body: The legendary Swiss marksman; Thoreau says the punctuality the railroad has taught everyone makes them all "sons of Tell."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Theseus
snapshots.body: The legendary Athenian hero, named alongside Hercules and Achilles in the quoted closing verses of Chapter 1 as an example of heroic virtue "for which antiquity hath left no name."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Old Mortality
snapshots.body: The title character of Walter Scott's novel, an old man who wanders Scotland re-cutting the inscriptions on covenanters' gravestones; Thoreau compares his philosopher-visitor to him, "say rather an Immortality."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: John Field
snapshots.body: An honest, hard-working, but shiftless Irish tenant farmer at the Baker Farm, visited during a thunderstorm in Chapter 10; Thoreau tries, without success, to persuade him that his laborious pursuit of tea, coffee, and meat is what keeps him poor.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Cato
snapshots.body: Marcus Porcius Cato the Elder, the Roman statesman and agricultural writer, quoted four times on farming and household management from his De Re Rustica -- including the recipe Thoreau follows for his own kneaded bread. Never confused in the text with Cato Ingraham, the formerly enslaved Concord resident of Chapter 14, who is bound separately and carries no global alias.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Cato Ingraham
snapshots.body: A formerly enslaved man, held by Duncan Ingraham of Concord village, who built him a house and let him live in Walden Woods; Thoreau notes the half-obliterated cellar hole that was his home, and that he is not to be confused with either Roman Cato -- "Cato, not Uticensis, but Concordiensis."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Brister Freeman
snapshots.body: A formerly enslaved man, "a handy Negro," held by Squire Cummings, who planted the apple trees still bearing wild fruit on Brister's Hill; his gravestone in the old Lincoln burying-ground styles him "Sippio Brister" -- a name Thoreau hears echoing Scipio Africanus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Fenda
snapshots.body: Brister Freeman's wife, "large, round, and black," who told fortunes hospitably and shared his house on Brister's Hill.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Zilpha
snapshots.body: A colored woman who spun linen for the townsfolk in a small house near Thoreau's bean-field, singing shrilly as she worked; her dwelling was burned by English prisoners of war in 1812 while she was away, killing her cat, dog, and hens.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hugh Quoil
snapshots.body: The last inhabitant of Walden Woods before Thoreau, an Irish ditcher known as "Col. Quoil," reputed to have fought at Waterloo; a man of manners and civil speech despite his poverty and trembling delirium, he died in the road at the foot of Brister's Hill shortly after Thoreau's arrival.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: John Farmer
snapshots.body: A parable figure of Chapter 11: a laborer who, resting after a hard day's work, hears a flute and feels called to a higher life than his "mean moiling" one, though he cannot see how to answer the call beyond a new austerity of mind.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hermit
snapshots.body: Thoreau's own voice in Chapter 12's staged dialogue -- a would-be contemplative interrupted mid-meditation by the Poet's proposal to go fishing, and unable to resist.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Poet
snapshots.body: The Hermit's fishing companion in Chapter 12's staged dialogue, identified with no other name; real-world scholarship reads him as Thoreau's friend and fellow writer William Ellery Channing, but the text itself never supplies that name.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Duncan Ingraham
snapshots.body: A gentleman of Concord village who enslaved Cato Ingraham and built him the house in Walden Woods where he was permitted to live.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Squire Cummings
snapshots.body: The Concord man who enslaved Brister Freeman.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: the Stratton family
snapshots.body: A former-inhabitant family whose homestead and orchard once covered the slope of Brister's Hill, named only by surname, with no individual member identified; not to be confused with Hezekiah Stratton, named later in the ledger excerpt of Chapter 15.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: the Breed family
snapshots.body: A former-inhabitant family whose hut, the site of a famous local house-fire Thoreau describes at length, stood near the edge of the wood closer to the village.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Nutting and Le Grosse
snapshots.body: Two former inhabitants named together, who lived where a well and lilac bushes still mark an open field; nothing else is told of them. Not to be confused with Sam Nutting, named later in Chapter 15.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Wyman the potter
snapshots.body: A potter who squatted farther into the woods than any other former inhabitant, furnished the town with earthenware, and left descendants who continued the trade after him; the last inhabitant before Hugh Quoil, who occupied "Wyman's tenement."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Wyman the younger
snapshots.body: Wyman the potter's descendant, who continued the family trade and later disappeared; a travelling pottery-dealer who had once bought a wheel from him stops to ask Thoreau what became of him.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Sam Nutting
snapshots.body: A bear-hunter on Fair Haven Ledges who traded skins for rum in Concord village and once claimed to have seen a moose there; owner of the famous fox-hound Burgoyne. Not to be confused with the unrelated former-inhabitant family of the same surname in Chapter 14.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Burgoyne
snapshots.body: Sam Nutting's famous fox-hound, borrowed by Thoreau's informant; Nutting himself pronounced the name "Bugine."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hezekiah Stratton
snapshots.body: A Concord man credited in an old trader's ledger with a wild-cat skin in 1743; a sergeant in the French war, and so not one who would have gotten credit for hunting less noble game. Not to be confused with the unrelated Stratton family of Chapter 14.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: John Melven
snapshots.body: A Concord man credited in an old trader's ledger with a grey fox skin in January 1742/3.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Mr. Gilian Baker
snapshots.body: A Lincoln farmer near the pond whose household kept an unusual "winged cat," which Thoreau visited and describes in Chapter 12.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Mr. Coleman
snapshots.body: Henry Coleman, the Massachusetts agricultural commissioner whose published farm reports Thoreau twice notes did not cover his bean-field.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Luther Blanchard
snapshots.body: A Concord Minuteman wounded at the Battle of Concord, invoked as a point of comparison in the mock-heroic account of Thoreau's ant battle.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Buttrick
snapshots.body: Major John Buttrick, who commanded the Concord Minutemen at the North Bridge; his order "Fire! for God's sake fire!" is echoed in the mock-heroic account of Thoreau's ant battle.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Davis and Hosmer
snapshots.body: Isaac Davis and Abner Hosmer, the two Concord Minutemen killed at the Battle of Concord, named together as the human dead whose fate the ant battle's carnage is mock-heroically compared to.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Homer
snapshots.body: The Greek epic poet; Thoreau keeps the Iliad on his table through the summer, reads a passage of it aloud in translation to a woodchopper acquaintance, and cites Alexander's habit of carrying it on campaign.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Æschylus
snapshots.body: The Greek tragedian, named alongside Homer as a classic never yet printed in English translation worth the name.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Virgil
snapshots.body: The Roman poet, named alongside Homer and Æschylus as a classic author.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Alexander
snapshots.body: Alexander the Great, who is said to have carried the Iliad with him on his expeditions in a precious casket.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Mîr Camar Uddîn Mast
snapshots.body: A poet Thoreau quotes on the pleasure of reading, comparing it to intoxication by wine.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Damodara
snapshots.body: An epithet of Krishna in Hindu scripture; Thoreau quotes a saying attributed to him about the freedom of a vast horizon, spoken when his herds needed new pastures.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: king Tching-thang
snapshots.body: A legendary Chinese emperor (Tang of Shang); Thoreau cites the characters said to be engraved on his bathing tub, urging daily renewal.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Confucius
snapshots.body: The Chinese philosopher, quoted several times under different transliterations of his name (Confucius, Khoung-tseu, Con-fut-see) on knowledge, virtue, and neighborliness.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Kieou-he-yu
snapshots.body: A great dignitary of the state of Wei, in the anecdote Thoreau quotes about sending a messenger to Confucius for news of his master.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Plato
snapshots.body: The Athenian philosopher; Thoreau reproaches himself for having his Dialogues on the shelf and never reading them, and later discusses Plato's definition of man as "a biped without feathers."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Zoroaster
snapshots.body: The ancient Persian religious teacher, invoked as an example of someone who had the same spiritual experience as a solitary hired man Thoreau knows, but treated it as universal wisdom rather than private singularity.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Jesus Christ
snapshots.body: Named as one through whose liberalizing influence, along with all the worthies, a solitary man might commune and set aside sectarian religion.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Abelard
snapshots.body: Peter Abelard, the medieval philosopher; Thoreau asks whether Concord could not hire some Abelard to lecture to it, as part of his argument that villages should fund culture as noblemen once did.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Adam
snapshots.body: The first man of Genesis, cited as the origin of human tedium and ennui, and, with Eve, of the first clothing (the bower) worn before the Fall.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Eve
snapshots.body: The first woman of Genesis, named with Adam as driven from Eden, and as first wearing the bower of Paradise before any other clothing.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Adam Smith
snapshots.body: The Scottish economist, named alongside Ricardo and Say as the "political economy" a poor student is taught in college while graduating in debt.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Ricardo
snapshots.body: David Ricardo, the British economist, named alongside Adam Smith and Say.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Say
snapshots.body: Jean-Baptiste Say, the French economist, named alongside Adam Smith and Ricardo. His surname also happens to be an ordinary English verb, capitalized twice elsewhere at the start of a sentence; only this one mention names the economist.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Sir Kenelm Digby
snapshots.body: The seventeenth-century English natural philosopher, quoted on the "vital spirits" attracted by fallow, exhausted soil.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Kirby
snapshots.body: William Kirby, co-author with Spence of a standard entomology text, cited on insects' feeding habits and on the history of recorded ant battles.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Spence
snapshots.body: William Spence, Kirby's co-author, cited alongside him.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Thseng-tseu
snapshots.body: Zengzi, a disciple of Confucius, quoted on the soul's absence from itself when the appetite masters perception: "one eats, and one does not know the savor of food."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Mencius
snapshots.body: The Chinese philosopher, quoted on the thin margin that distinguishes men from brute beasts, and how easily the common herd loses it.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Chaucer’s nun
snapshots.body: The Canterbury Tales narrator Thoreau quotes and attributes to "Chaucer's nun," on hunters not being unholy men. Chaucer's own name never appears in the text on its own -- only as part of this one phrase -- so there is no separate entry for Chaucer himself.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Huber
snapshots.body: François Huber, the Swiss entomologist Kirby and Spence credit as the only modern author to have witnessed a battle of ants firsthand.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Æneas Sylvius
snapshots.body: Aeneas Sylvius Piccolomini, later Pope Pius II, quoted by Kirby and Spence for his circumstantial account of a battle of ants on a pear tree.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Eugenius the Fourth
snapshots.body: Pope Eugene IV, in whose pontificate the ant battle Æneas Sylvius describes is said to have taken place.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Nicholas Pistoriensis
snapshots.body: An eminent lawyer said to have witnessed and related the history of the ant battle Æneas Sylvius describes.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Olaus Magnus
snapshots.body: The Swedish churchman and writer who records a second ant battle, quoted by Kirby and Spence.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Christiern the Second
snapshots.body: Christian II of Denmark, the "tyrant" whose expulsion from Sweden the ant battle Olaus Magnus describes is said to have preceded.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Polk
snapshots.body: James K. Polk, President of the United States when Thoreau's own witnessed ant battle took place, per his mock-scholarly dating of the event.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Webster
snapshots.body: Daniel Webster, whose Fugitive-Slave Bill dates Thoreau's ant battle in Chapter 12, and who is later named, in Chapter 18, as the orator of an imagined national celebration presided over by God.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Samuel Laing
snapshots.body: The travel writer quoted on Laplanders sleeping unclothed on snow in reindeer-skin bags.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Winslow
snapshots.body: Edward Winslow, later governor of the Plymouth Colony, whose account of a diplomatic visit to Massasoit -- warmly received but poorly fed and lodged -- Thoreau quotes at length.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Massasoit
snapshots.body: The Wampanoag sachem who received Winslow's Plymouth delegation, sharing what little food his people had.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Benvenuto Cellini
snapshots.body: The Italian Renaissance artist and memoirist, whose account of a halo seen over his own shadow after a vision in prison Thoreau compares to a phenomenon he has observed himself.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Guy Faux
snapshots.body: Guy Fawkes, the Gunpowder Plot conspirator, named in a quoted poem about the Baker Farm.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: William Gilpin
snapshots.body: The English writer on landscape aesthetics, quoted on the dimensions and origin of Scotland's Loch Fyne, used as a point of comparison for Walden's own depth.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Michaux
snapshots.body: François André Michaux, the French botanist, quoted on the high price of firewood in early-nineteenth-century New York and Philadelphia.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Nebuchadnezzar
snapshots.body: The Babylonian king; Thoreau notes, of his second-hand chimney bricks, that he did not find this name inscribed on them, unlike the ancient bricks of Babylon that supply Mesopotamian villages with building material.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Franklin
snapshots.body: Sir John Franklin, the British Arctic explorer whose lost expedition was a major contemporary news story; Thoreau asks pointedly whether he is "the only man who is lost."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Mr. Grinnell
snapshots.body: Henry Grinnell, the American philanthropist who funded search expeditions for Sir John Franklin.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Mungo Park
snapshots.body: The Scottish explorer of West Africa, named among the explorers Thoreau urges his reader to become instead within their own mind.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Lewis
snapshots.body: Meriwether Lewis, of the Lewis and Clark expedition, named among the explorers of Chapter 18's closing exhortation.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Clarke
snapshots.body: William Clark, of the Lewis and Clark expedition, named alongside Lewis.

snapshots.name: Columbus
snapshots.body: Christopher Columbus, invoked as the model for exploring continents and worlds within oneself rather than geographic ones.

snapshots.name: Mirabeau
snapshots.body: The Comte de Mirabeau, quoted on having taken to highway robbery to test what resolution was needed to defy society's most sacred laws -- a resolve Thoreau calls manly but idle.

snapshots.name: Kabir
snapshots.body: The Indian poet-saint, whose verses are said to admit four different senses -- cited as a contrast to the demand, in Thoreau's own place and time, that writing admit only one interpretation.

snapshots.name: Crœsus
snapshots.body: The proverbially wealthy king of Lydia, invoked to argue that even his riches would not change what a person's true aims and means must be.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Tom Hyde
snapshots.body: A tinker, hanged, whose last words on the gallows -- reminding tailors to knot their thread before the first stitch -- Thoreau offers as an example of truth over decorum.

snapshots.name: Champollion
snapshots.body: Jean-François Champollion, decipherer of Egyptian hieroglyphics, invoked rhetorically to ask who will decipher the "hieroglyphic" of the sand foliage on the railroad bank.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Calidas
snapshots.body: Kalidasa, the classical Sanskrit poet and dramatist, whose play Sacontala Thoreau quotes for its image of golden pollen-dust.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Jupiter
snapshots.body: The chief god of the Roman pantheon; commerce, Thoreau notes, does not clasp its hands and pray to him, and Hebe, cupbearer to Jupiter, is invoked as a symbol of perpetual youth and health.

snapshots.name: Ceres
snapshots.body: The Roman goddess of agriculture, to whom -- Thoreau argues -- modern farmers no longer sacrifice, worshipping the infernal Plutus instead.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Plutus
snapshots.body: The Greek god of wealth, whom Thoreau says the modern farmer serves in place of Ceres.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Saturn
snapshots.body: The Roman god of a legendary golden age, named as the ancestral king whose race the old Romans believed themselves alone left of, and again as the "prostrate Saturn of an older dynasty" one steps over on entering Thoreau's imagined communal hall.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Minerva
snapshots.body: The Roman goddess of wisdom, invoked in an anecdote about her objection to a house Momus criticized for not being movable, and again as the master builder of an oil-and-wine-cellar-equipped villa.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Aurora
snapshots.body: The Roman goddess of the dawn; Thoreau calls himself as sincere a worshipper of her as the Greeks, and all poets and heroes are called her children.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Memnon
snapshots.body: The mythological son of Aurora, a byword for a statue that sang at dawn; invoked as the type of all poets and heroes, children of Aurora who emit their music at sunrise.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hygeia
snapshots.body: The Greek goddess of health, daughter of Æsculapius; Thoreau declines to worship her, preferring Hebe instead.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Æsculapius
snapshots.body: The Greek and Roman god of medicine, named as Hygeia's father, "that old herb-doctor."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hebe
snapshots.body: The Roman goddess of youth, cupbearer to Jupiter and daughter of Juno; Thoreau prefers her worship to Hygeia's, calling her the power to restore gods and men to the vigor of youth.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Juno
snapshots.body: The Roman queen of the gods, named as Hebe's mother.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Atlas
snapshots.body: The Titan condemned to bear the world on his shoulders, invoked when Thoreau describes his own eagerness to improve the Hollowell farm.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hercules
snapshots.body: The Greek and Roman demigod hero; his twelve labors are compared, unfavorably, to the burdens Thoreau's Concord neighbors have undertaken, and his strength is invoked again when Thoreau feels "strength like Antæus" from his beans.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Cerberus
snapshots.body: The three-headed dog guarding the underworld in Greek myth, invoked as a figure for any host's overbearing insistence on feeding a guest.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Vulcan
snapshots.body: The Roman god of fire, to whom Thoreau says he sacrificed an old forest fence for firewood.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Terminus
snapshots.body: The Roman god of boundaries, whom an old forest fence, past its usefulness, was said no longer to serve.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Brahma
snapshots.body: The Hindu creator god, invoked in the parable of the artist of Kouroo, whose perfect staff becomes, at the moment of completion, one of the fairest of all of Brahma's creations.

snapshots.name: Vishnu
snapshots.body: The Hindu preserver god, named alongside Brahma and Indra as a deity the servant of a Brahmin priest is said to worship.

snapshots.name: Indra
snapshots.body: The Hindu king of the gods, named alongside Brahma and Vishnu, and invoked earlier as the detached spectator in the sky Thoreau imagines himself as, watching the stream of events from above.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Thor
snapshots.body: The Norse god of thunder, whose hammer -- which only breaks things in pieces -- is contrasted with the gentler, more powerful persuasion of the spring thaw.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Atropos
snapshots.body: One of the three Fates in Greek myth, who cuts the thread of life; Thoreau proposes her name for the unstoppable railroad engine, "a fate ... that never turns aside."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Ulysses
snapshots.body: The hero of Homer's Odyssey, invoked as the model for sailing past the daily "whirlpool" of dinner "tied to the mast," resisting distraction.

snapshots.name: Achilles
snapshots.body: The hero of Homer's Iliad; Thoreau translates his rebuke to Patroclus aloud to a woodchopper acquaintance, and later imagines a red ant as "some Achilles" avenging a fallen companion in the battle of the ants.

snapshots.name: Patroclus
snapshots.body: Achilles' companion in the Iliad, whose sad countenance Achilles rebukes in the passage Thoreau translates aloud, and whom the avenging red ant of the battle scene is compared to avenging.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Menœtius
snapshots.body: Patroclus's father, named in the Iliad passage Thoreau translates.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Peleus
snapshots.body: Achilles' father, named in the same Iliad passage.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Æacus
snapshots.body: Peleus's father and Achilles' grandfather, named in the same Iliad passage.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: the Myrmidons
snapshots.body: Achilles' warriors in the Iliad, named in the translated passage; Thoreau later calls the legions of battling ants in his wood-yard "these Myrmidons."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Antæus
snapshots.body: The giant of Greek myth who drew his strength from contact with the earth; Thoreau says he got strength like his from cultivating his bean rows.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: the Sirens
snapshots.body: The mythological singers whose voices lured sailors to their deaths; Thoreau says he escapes the village's gossip by keeping his thoughts on high things, "like Orpheus," who drowned their voices with his own song.

snapshots.name: Orpheus
snapshots.body: The legendary musician of Greek myth, whose singing drowned out the Sirens' voices and kept him out of danger, a model Thoreau invokes for escaping the village's gossip.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Robinhood
snapshots.body: The legendary English outlaw, named among those across history and rank who have all required a few sticks from the forest to warm them and cook their food.

snapshots.name: Goody Blake
snapshots.body: A character from Wordsworth's poem "Goody Blake and Harry Gill," named alongside Harry Gill in the same passage as Robinhood.

snapshots.name: Harry Gill
snapshots.body: The other title character of Wordsworth's poem, named alongside Goody Blake.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Actæon
snapshots.body: The mythological hunter torn apart by his own hounds; Thoreau notes that the woods ring with hunting cries yet no fox bursts forth "pursuing their Actæon."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Toscar
snapshots.body: A figure from the Ossianic poems, named as the father of the "beautiful daughter" mourned in a quoted verse.

snapshots.name: Pilpay
snapshots.body: The legendary Indian fabulist credited with the beast-fables of the Panchatantra, invoked (as "Pilpay & Co.") for having put animals to their best literary use as vehicles for human thought.

snapshots.name: Robin Goodfellow
snapshots.body: The mischievous sprite of English folklore (later Shakespeare's Puck), invoked as a figure for an erratic, meddling sun that helps by fits and starts rather than steadily.

snapshots.name: Reynard
snapshots.body: The fox of medieval beast-fable tradition, invoked generically for the fox a black chicken at Hugh Quoil's abandoned house is said to be "awaiting."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Tell
snapshots.body: The legendary Swiss marksman; Thoreau says the punctuality the railroad has taught everyone makes them all "sons of Tell."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Theseus
snapshots.body: The legendary Athenian hero, named alongside Hercules and Achilles in the quoted closing verses of Chapter 1 as an example of heroic virtue "for which antiquity hath left no name."

snapshots.name: Old Mortality
snapshots.body: The title character of Walter Scott's novel, an old man who wanders Scotland re-cutting the inscriptions on covenanters' gravestones; Thoreau compares his philosopher-visitor to him, "say rather an Immortality."
